body: On November 5, 2026, the Tenth District Court of Appeals of Ohio reversed a Franklin County Court of Common Pleas judgment in an eminent domain case brought by the City of Columbus, holding that the trial court was wrong to bar a mortgage lender, Wiltshire Capital Partners, LP, from claiming an interest in the property. Judge Dingus wrote the decision, and Judges Edelstein and Leland concurred.

In August 2021 the city petitioned to appropriate a fee simple interest and a temporary easement on a 0.082-acre parcel, and a temporary construction easement on a 0.016-acre parcel, for the Hudson Street Sidewalks Project. It named nine parties with possible interests, including the fee owner, Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales, LLC, and Wiltshire as a mortgagee of record. By April 2022 only Wiltshire, Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales and the Franklin County Treasurer remained. Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales pointed out that Wiltshire had filed a foreclosure on the same mortgage in August 2017, which the court dismissed in March 2018 for failure to prosecute after Wiltshire did not obtain service. In July 2023 the trial court ruled that res judicata barred Wiltshire's claim and that Wiltshire lacked standing. Wiltshire's first appeal was dismissed in 2024 for lack of a final, appealable order, although the appellate court noted that the issue was not really one of standing, since the city itself had named Wiltshire as a respondent.

In May 2025 the trial court approved the city's settlement with Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales over Wiltshire's objection and vested title in the city upon a $4,014 payment to the owner. It also agreed with the owner that Wiltshire had failed to set forth an interest in the property, citing an apparent assignment of the note underlying the mortgage.

On the second appeal, the panel noted that Ohio Civil Rule 41(B)(3) generally treats a dismissal for failure to prosecute as an adjudication on the merits unless the court says otherwise. But under the Ohio Supreme Court's decision in Thomas v. Freeman, when a plaintiff has not obtained service on the defendant, a dismissal under either Civil Rule 41(B)(1) or Civil Rule 4(E) is otherwise than on the merits. Wiltshire had served only the county treasurer in the 2017 case, not the owner, so that dismissal was without prejudice and could not bar its claim. The court said it made no finding on whether Wiltshire holds a valid and enforceable mortgage, and directed that Wiltshire be allowed to assert its claim and argue those issues on remand. It treated Wiltshire's remaining assignments of error as moot.

timeline.label: Wiltshire Capital Partners files a foreclosure action on its mortgage
Foreclosure dismissed for failure to prosecute after Wiltshire does not obtain service
City of Columbus files its appropriation petition for the Hudson Street Sidewalks Project
Trial court rules res judicata bars Wiltshire's mortgage claim
Tenth District dismisses Wiltshire's first appeal for lack of a final, appealable order
Trial court approves the city's settlement with the owner and vests title on a $4,014 payment
Tenth District reverses and remands, holding the 2018 dismissal was not on the merits
